title: KV cache compression and quantization
summary: Why the KV cache caps batch size and context, and the three ways to shrink it: share heads (MQA, GQA), use fewer bits (KIVI, KVQuant, FP8), or keep fewer tokens (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV).
outcomes: Compute KV cache bytes per token and per batch from a real model config such as Llama 3 8B
Explain how MQA and GQA shrink the cache and why they require (up)training
Explain why keys are quantized per channel and values per token, and compute the overhead of scales
Explain how pre-RoPE keys, outlier handling and FP8 scales keep quantization error low
Compare sliding windows, attention sinks, H2O, SnapKV and PyramidKV and pick one for a workload

lessons.title: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size

blocks.md: From the prerequisite course you know the **KV cache**: during decoding, every layer keeps the key and value vectors of every earlier token so they are not recomputed. Its size is fixed by the model's shape, the number of tokens, and the bytes used per number.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes per value}
blocks.caption: The 2 counts one key and one value vector per KV head per layer.

blocks.md: Plug in a real model. The Hugging Face `config.json` of **Llama 3 8B** lists `num_hidden_layers: 32`, `num_attention_heads: 32`, `num_key_value_heads: 8` and `hidden_size: 4096`, so each head has $d_{\text{head}} = 4096 / 32 = 128$. The Llama 3 paper's Table 3 gives the same shape. In BF16 (2 bytes):

blocks.prompt: Llama 3 8B's config has max_position_embeddings 8192. Serve a batch of 32 sequences, each 8192 tokens long. Is the KV cache bigger or smaller than the roughly 16 GB of BF16 weights?
blocks.reveal: **About twice as big.** One 8192-token sequence needs $128 \text{ KiB} \times 8192 = 1$ GiB (1.07 GB). Times 32 sequences that is 32 GiB, or **34.4 GB**, against **16.1 GB** of weights (8.03 billion parameters, counted from the same config, at 2 bytes each). The weights are shared by every request; the cache is per request, so it is what grows with batch and context.

blocks.title: KV cache of Llama 3 8B vs context length

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B as shipped: 8 KV heads, BF16, batch 8. The cache grows linearly with context and crosses the 63.9 GB left on an 80 GB GPU after weights near 61K tokens per sequence.
Counterfactual: the same model with one KV head per query head (32, plain multi-head attention). Every point is 4x higher; batch 8 runs out of memory near 15K tokens.
Back to 8 KV heads, but store the cache in FP8 (1 byte). The line halves, so twice the tokens or twice the batch fit.
2-bit values plus one FP16 scale and zero point per 32 numbers is about 3 bits, or 0.375 bytes. Simplified: real systems also need activation memory and allocator slack.

blocks.md: The formula hands you the levers. You can shrink $n_{\text{kv heads}}$ (share keys and values across query heads, lesson 2), shrink bytes per value (**quantization**, lessons 3 and 4), or shrink the number of tokens kept (**eviction**, lessons 5 and 6). The first is decided when the model is trained; the other two can be applied at serving time.

Memory is only half the story. In the prerequisite course you saw that each decode step must read the whole cache from HBM. A cache that is 4x smaller is also 4x fewer bytes to stream per step, so compression can raise speed as well as capacity, if the kernels read the compressed form directly.
KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.
A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

blocks.question: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, and stores its cache in FP8. How many bytes per token?
blocks.explain: $2 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1 = 81{,}920$ bytes. 163,840 forgets that FP8 is 1 byte, 655,360 uses 32 heads at 2 bytes, and 40,960 drops the factor of 2 for keys plus values.

blocks.question: You double the batch size and halve the context length per request. What happens to the total KV cache?
blocks.explain: Total cache is proportional to batch x tokens per sequence. $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so the cache is unchanged, though per-step attention work per sequence drops.

lessons.title: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA

blocks.md: In standard **multi-head attention (MHA)** each of the $H$ query heads has its own key head and value head, so the cache stores $H$ key and $H$ value vectors per layer per token. Shazeer's 2019 paper *Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need* observed that incremental decoding is slow because of the memory bandwidth spent repeatedly loading these large key and value tensors.

**Multi-query attention (MQA)** keeps all $H$ query heads but shares a **single** key head and value head across them. The cache shrinks by a factor of $H$. The paper reports much faster decoding with only minor quality degradation.

**Grouped-query attention (GQA)**, from Ainslie et al. (2023), interpolates. Query heads are split into $G$ groups and each group shares one key and value head. GQA-1 is MQA and GQA-$H$ is MHA. Llama 3 uses GQA with 8 KV heads; its paper says this was done to improve inference speed and reduce KV cache size during decoding.

blocks.title: 8 query heads sharing KV heads (toy, one layer)

scenes.caption: GQA with 4 groups: each pair of query heads reads one shared KV head. The cache holds 4 key and 4 value vectors per token in this layer instead of 8.
MQA (GQA-1): all 8 query heads read the same KV head. The cache is 8x smaller than MHA, but every head must now attend using identical keys and values.

Llama 3 8B mapped onto this picture: read each circle as 2 of its 32 query heads and each cylinder as 1 of its 8 KV heads (half a layer shown). Each KV head serves 4 query heads, so the cache is a quarter of MHA's.

blocks.title: Llama 3 8B shape: KiB per token, then sequences that fit

scenes.caption: Same 32 layers, head size 128 and BF16 for all three; only the KV head count changes. 512, 128 and 16 KiB per token.
Max 8192-token sequences in the 63.9 GB left after weights on an 80 GB GPU (simplified, ignoring activations): 14 for MHA, 59 for GQA-8, and about 476 for MQA.

blocks.md: Why not always use MQA? The GQA paper notes that MQA can degrade quality, and that training a separate model just for faster inference may not be desirable. Its recipe **uptrains** an existing MHA checkpoint: mean-pool the key and value projection matrices within each group into one head, then continue pre-training for about 5% of the original compute. Uptrained GQA reached quality close to MHA with speed close to MQA. For their large model the authors chose 8 groups as a middle ground.
GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.
GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

blocks.question: A team wants to cut KV memory of an already-deployed MHA model by 4x tomorrow, with no training budget. Which is a realistic option?
options: Switch the config to 4x fewer KV heads
Uptrain to GQA with 5% of pre-training compute overnight
Quantize the cache from 16 to about 4 bits
blocks.explain: Changing num_key_value_heads without uptraining gives weights that no longer match the architecture. Uptraining costs 5% of the original pre-training run, far from overnight. Quantizing the cache needs no training, which is why the next lessons focus on it.

blocks.question: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, what does each KV head serve?
options: One query head; the other 24 are unused
blocks.explain: Query heads are split into 8 groups of 4, and each group shares one key head and one value head.

lessons.title: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)

blocks.md: **Quantization** stores each number as a small integer plus shared scaling information. The simplest scheme is asymmetric **round-to-nearest**: a group of numbers shares a **scale** $s$ and a **zero point** $z$, and each number becomes an integer code $q$ between $0$ and $2^b - 1$ for $b$ bits.

blocks.tex: z = \min(X),\quad s = \frac{\max(X) - \min(X)}{2^b - 1},\quad q = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{x - z}{s}\right),\quad \hat{x} = q\,s + z
blocks.caption: Asymmetric b-bit quantization of one group X. Dequantization gives back an approximation x-hat.

blocks.md: The design question is which numbers share a group. The cache for one head is a matrix with one row per **token** and one column per **channel** (a coordinate of the head vector). **Per-token** quantization groups a row; **per-channel** quantization groups a column. The KIVI paper (Liu et al., 2024) studied KV caches of real models and found that keys have a few fixed **outlier channels** with very large magnitude, while values show no obvious outlier pattern.

blocks.title: Toy key cache: 6 tokens x 6 channels, 2-bit

scenes.caption: Toy keys shaped like the KIVI finding: channel c3 is an outlier channel near 10 for every token; the rest sit in [-1, 1]. Real heads have 128 channels.
Per-token 2-bit: each row shares one range, which c3 stretches to about 10, so the step is 3.2 to 3.9. Almost every small entry collapses to the row minimum. MSE 0.84.
Per-channel 2-bit: each column gets its own range. c3 spans only 8.7 to 11.2 and the small channels keep their own fine steps. MSE 0.026, about 33x lower, at the same 2 bits.
Back to the original keys for comparison. The outlier is confined to its own column, so per-channel groups keep its error out of the other channels.

blocks.md: Why do keys matter so much? Attention scores are $q \cdot k$. Take a toy query $q = (1, -1, 0.5, 0.1, -0.5, 1)$ that mostly ignores the outlier channel, as many heads do, and compare softmax weights over the 6 tokens computed from the original and the two quantized key caches (scaled by $1/\sqrt{6}$).

blocks.title: Attention weights of one query over the 6 toy keys

scenes.caption: Exact keys: tokens t0, t2 and t4 get about 0.29, 0.29 and 0.27 of the attention.
Per-token 2-bit keys: small channels were erased, so the pattern is scrambled. t2 jumps to 0.39 and t0 falls to 0.11.
Per-channel 2-bit keys: weights stay within 0.03 of exact (0.29, 0.06, 0.26, 0.05, 0.30, 0.04).

blocks.md: Values are used differently: the attention output is a weighted mix of value **rows**. KIVI argues that per-token quantization confines each value's error to its own token, so a token with low attention weight contributes little error. Their simulated test on Llama-2-13B (group size 32, CoQA score) makes the asymmetry concrete: 16-bit scored 66.37; 2-bit with keys per-channel and values per-token scored 63.53; 2-bit with both per-token scored 52.93; both per-channel scored 2.88; keys per-token and values per-channel scored 2.80.

blocks.prompt: Per-channel grouping needs a group of tokens, but decoding produces one token at a time. How can you quantize a key channel when only 5 new tokens have arrived?
blocks.reveal: You cannot form the group yet. KIVI splits the cache into a **grouped** part, already quantized, and a **residual** part of recent tokens kept in **full precision**. When the residual reaches $R$ tokens (128 in their experiments, a multiple of the group size 32), keys are quantized per-channel as a block and appended. Values use a queue: the oldest full-precision value is popped, quantized per-token, and appended. Attention combines both parts with tiled matrix multiplication.

blocks.title: KIVI key cache during decoding (toy residual length R = 4)

scenes.caption: After 3 tokens: all keys sit in the full-precision residual (fp). No group of 4 exists yet.
Token 4 fills the residual. The 4 keys are quantized per-channel to 2 bits as one block (q2) and the residual is emptied.
Tokens 5 to 7 accumulate in a fresh residual. Attention reads 4 quantized keys plus 3 full-precision ones.
At token 8 the second block is quantized. Simplified: KIVI uses R = 128 and groups of 32, so up to 128 recent tokens stay in full precision.

blocks.md: The scales and zero points cost memory too. With one FP16 scale and one FP16 zero point per group of 32 numbers, overhead is $32 / 32 = 1$ extra bit per number, so 2-bit codes cost about 3 bits each. For Llama 3 8B that is $128 \times 3/16 = 24$ KiB per token instead of 128. The KIVI paper reports 2.6x less peak memory including weights, up to 4x larger batch, and 2.35x to 3.47x throughput on Llama, Falcon and Mistral.

Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.
Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

blocks.question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
blocks.explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

blocks.question: In the toy, per-channel 2-bit keys reached MSE 0.026 while per-token 4-bit keys reached 0.028. What does this suggest?
options: Bit width matters more than grouping axis
Choosing the right axis can matter as much as two extra bits
The toy is broken, since 4 bits must always win
Outlier channels only matter for values
blocks.explain: With the right grouping, 2 bits matched what per-token needed 4 bits for, because the range of each group no longer includes the outlier. 4 bits does not win automatically when its groups mix scales.

lessons.title: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production

blocks.md: **KVQuant** (Hooper et al., 2024) pushes below 4 bits with several additions. It keeps per-channel key quantization and adds: quantizing keys **before RoPE**, per-layer non-uniform number formats, keeping a small fraction of **outliers** in a separate sparse full-precision store, and keeping the first token in FP16. The paper reports under 0.1 perplexity degradation at 3 bits on Wikitext-2 and C4 for LLaMA, Llama-2, Llama-3 and Mistral.

**RoPE** (rotary position embedding) rotates each pair of key channels by an angle proportional to the token's position. That helps attention know relative positions, but it mixes the two channels of a pair by a different amount at every position. A channel that had a steady large value before RoPE swings between large positive, near zero and large negative afterwards.

blocks.title: One channel pair before and after RoPE (toy: 0.5 rad per position)

scenes.caption: Before RoPE, channel a is steady near 8 and b is near 0. Each column has a narrow range, ideal for per-channel groups.
After RoPE, the pair is rotated by 0.5 rad x position. Column a now spans -6.77 to 8.0 and b spans 0.3 to 8.19: the steady outlier became a swinging one.

blocks.title: Per-channel quantization MSE on the toy pair

scenes.caption: Same 12 numbers, same per-channel scheme. Quantizing before rotation gives 0.004 vs 0.93 at 2 bits, and 0.001 vs 0.12 at 3 bits. Rotation preserves length, so pre-RoPE error stays the same after RoPE is applied.

blocks.md: The catch is that the cache then holds un-rotated keys, so RoPE must be applied after dequantization on every read. KVQuant writes a fused kernel to do this on the fly, and reports a 0.82 perplexity improvement on Wikitext-2 for 3-bit LLaMA-7B from pre-RoPE quantization alone.

Two more KVQuant pieces target rare large values. **Dense-and-sparse** quantization pulls the largest-magnitude values of each vector out into a sparse full-precision list, so they no longer stretch the range of the rest; removing 1% of values this way gave a further 0.19 perplexity gain for 3-bit LLaMA-7B. And because of the **attention sink** effect (models put large attention on the first token, lesson 5), the model is disproportionately sensitive to error in that token, so KVQuant keeps the first token in FP16.

Production engines mostly ship a simpler option: an **FP8** cache. vLLM's `kv_cache_dtype` accepts `"fp8"`, `"fp8_e4m3"` and `"fp8_e5m2"`, and supports a per-tensor scale or, with calibration from llm-compressor, per-attention-head scales. Without calibration, all scales default to 1.0. TensorRT-LLM supports INT8 and FP8 KV caches with a per-tensor `kv_cache_scaling_factor` of shape [1]; values are quantized when written and dequantized on the fly inside the attention kernel.

blocks.code:
from vllm import LLM

# BF16 weights, FP8 (e4m3) KV cache: half the bytes per cached token.
llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
          kv_cache_dtype="fp8")
# Without calibrated scales, vLLM uses scale 1.0 for K and V.
# For calibrated per-tensor or per-head scales, quantize the
# checkpoint with llm-compressor first (see the vLLM docs).
blocks.caption: Enabling an FP8 KV cache in vLLM, following its quantized KV cache docs.

blocks.title: FP8 KV cache: quantize on write, dequantize on read

nodes.label:
multiply by 1 / scale,
cast to FP8

scenes.caption: Write path: each new token's keys and values are scaled and cast to FP8 once, when they enter the cache.
Read path: every decode step streams the FP8 cache, half the bytes of BF16, and dequantizes inside the attention kernel (TensorRT-LLM's description).
Variation: vLLM notes that with the FlashAttention 3 backend and an FP8 cache, attention itself runs in FP8 and queries are quantized too.

blocks.md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones) can be kept in the native dtype.

blocks.question: Why does KVQuant quantize keys before applying RoPE?
options: RoPE rotates channel pairs by position-dependent angles, so a steady outlier channel becomes inconsistent across tokens
RoPE makes keys larger, which overflows FP16
RoPE is only applied to values
Post-RoPE keys cannot be cached at all
blocks.explain: Per-channel quantization relies on each channel having a consistent range across tokens. Position-dependent rotation spreads a large channel's energy into its partner, widening both ranges. The cost is reapplying RoPE after dequantization.

blocks.question: Your FP8 KV cache (no calibration) is accurate on most layers but one sliding-window layer degrades. Which change targets that directly?
options: Keep that layer's cache in the native dtype and the rest in FP8
blocks.explain: vLLM documents a skip-layers option for exactly this: sensitive layers stay in the model's dtype while the rest use the quantized cache.

lessons.title: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters

blocks.md: Quantization keeps every token but stores each one more cheaply. **Eviction** keeps a fixed **budget** of tokens and drops the rest. The bet is that attention is sparse: the H2O paper (Zhang et al., 2023) reports that attention matrices of LLMs are over 95% sparse at inference time, so most cached tokens get almost no weight.

The obvious policy is a **sliding window**: keep the most recent $W$ tokens. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) showed that it fails badly once text exceeds the window. Llama-2-13B on a 65K-token book had perplexity 5158 with a 1024-token window, but 5.40 when the cache kept the first 4 tokens plus the 1020 most recent.

The reason is the **attention sink**: models put large attention on the first few tokens even when they are not semantically important, apparently as a place to park attention that softmax forces to sum to 1. Evict them and the attention distribution shifts. StreamingLLM found 1 or 2 initial tokens are not enough and 4 generally suffice.

**H2O** (Heavy-Hitter Oracle) adds content awareness. It sums each cached token's attention scores over the steps so far; tokens with large sums are **heavy hitters**. The cache keeps a balance of heavy hitters and recent tokens, and when full it evicts the non-recent token with the smallest accumulated score. The paper finds keeping only heavy hitters or only recent tokens is worse than both together.

Toy setup for the figure (synthetic logits, computed by script): 12 tokens; token 0 is a sink, tokens 2 and 5 carry key content, and the last two tokens get a recency boost. Budget: 5 cached tokens plus the current one. Rows are the queries of tokens 6 to 11; columns are keys 0 to 11. Values are full-cache attention weights.

blocks.title: Which keys each policy can still see (budget 5 + current)

scenes.caption: Full cache. Most weight lands on token 0 (0.30 to 0.48), token 2 (0.12 to 0.17) and token 5 (0.14 to 0.18, and 0.49 for q6, where it is also recent); the rest is a thin recency diagonal.
Sliding window: only the 6 most recent keys. Token 0 is gone from the first row on, then 2 and 5. On average only 43% of the full attention weight is still visible.
StreamingLLM style: token 0 kept as a sink plus the 4 most recent. The sink alone restores much of the mass (78%), but tokens 2 and 5 still fall out of the window.
H2O: 2 recent slots plus 3 slots for the highest accumulated scores. From q8 on, tokens 0, 2 and 5 hold those slots; visible mass is 93%.
Mass kept is the share of full-cache attention weight on visible keys. Output error compares the attention output (1-dimensional toy values) with and without eviction, averaged over the 6 queries.

blocks.prompt: In the H2O run, token 3 had an accumulated score of 0.23 and was evicted when token 8 arrived, while token 0 had 4.36. Suppose the user's next question is about the content of token 3. What happens?
blocks.reveal: It is gone for good. Eviction is **irreversible**: H2O decided from past attention, and a token that was unimportant so far can become crucial later. Quantization degrades every token a little; eviction loses some tokens completely. That is why retrieval-style tests (finding one fact in a long document) are the standard stress test for eviction methods.

blocks.md: One more detail makes StreamingLLM work: positions are assigned **within the cache**, not in the original text. With cached tokens [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8] and token 9 being decoded, the positions used are 0 to 7. For RoPE models it caches keys before rotation and applies RoPE at each step, the same pre-RoPE idea as KVQuant for a different reason.
Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

blocks.question: A chat service uses a pure 4096-token sliding window. After the conversation passes 4096 tokens, output turns to gibberish. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Also keep the first few tokens as attention sinks
Recompute the whole window every step
blocks.explain: The collapse begins when the initial tokens leave the window, so the softmax loses its sink. Keeping 4 initial tokens restored Llama-2-13B from perplexity 5158 to 5.40 in StreamingLLM. A bigger window only delays the failure.

blocks.question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
blocks.explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

lessons.title: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe

blocks.md: H2O decides token by token during decoding. For long prompts (documents, code, retrieval context) most of the cache is created at once during prefill. **SnapKV** (Li et al., 2024) compresses it right after prefill. It found that each attention head keeps focusing on the same prompt positions during generation, and that this pattern can be read from an **observation window**: the last few tokens of the prompt.

Per head, SnapKV sums the attention that the observation-window queries give to each earlier prompt token (a **vote**), smooths the votes with 1D max pooling so neighbors of a peak are kept as a cluster, keeps the top-scoring positions, and appends the window itself. The paper's LongBench runs use an observation window of 32 and a max-pooling kernel of 7 (16 and 5 in its needle-in-a-haystack and pooling ablation runs); the figure below uses a toy window of 3 and kernel of 3.

blocks.title: SnapKV selection on a 12-token toy prompt
blocks.code:
def snapkv(attn, window, budget, kernel):
    # attn: [prompt_len, prompt_len] for one head
    obs = attn[-window:, :-window]       # window queries vs prefix keys
    vote = obs.sum(axis=0)               # total attention per prefix token
    pooled = max_pool1d(vote, kernel)    # spread peaks to neighbors
    keep = topk(pooled, budget - window) # pick prefix positions
    n = attn.shape[0]
    return sorted(keep) + list(range(n - window, n))

scenes.caption: Prompt of 12 tokens; tokens 9 to 11 form the observation window. Budget 6: the window plus 3 prefix tokens.
Votes sum the attention from the 3 window queries to prefix tokens 0 to 8. Token 5 is the clear peak; token 8 is an isolated spike.
Max pooling with kernel 3 gives 4 and 6 the peak score of their neighbor 5. Without pooling, top-3 would be [4, 5, 8], splitting the cluster.
Top-3 of the pooled votes keeps the whole cluster [4, 5, 6]. Final cache: 6 of 12 tokens. The paper argues clusters preserve details, such as a full phone number.

blocks.md: SnapKV reports a 3.6x increase in generation speed and 8.2x better memory efficiency at 16K-token inputs, and processing up to 380K tokens on one A100-80GB with a negligible drop in a needle-in-a-haystack test.

**PyramidKV** (Cai et al., 2024) observes that attention is spread widely in lower layers and concentrates on a few tokens in higher layers. So instead of the same budget per layer, it gives lower layers more. With a total budget $k^{\text{total}}$ over $m$ layers and a shape hyperparameter $\beta$, the top layer gets $k^{\text{total}}/(\beta m)$, the bottom layer gets $2k^{\text{total}}/m$ minus that, and layers in between follow an arithmetic sequence. Token selection inside each layer follows SnapKV.

blocks.title: Per-layer KV budget for a toy 8-layer model (average 64)

scenes.caption: Uniform allocation, as in SnapKV or H2O: 64 tokens in every layer, 512 in total.
PyramidKV with beta = 4: top layer 512 / (4 x 8) = 16, bottom 2 x 512 / 8 - 16 = 112, a straight line in between. Still 512 in total.

blocks.md: The paper reports matching full-cache LongBench performance while keeping 12% of the KV cache.
Putting the course together for Llama 3 8B on an 80 GB GPU with 8192-token sequences (63.9 GB left after weights, ignoring activations and allocator overheads):

blocks.title: Llama 3 8B: 8192-token sequences that fit in 63.9 GB

scenes.caption: Simplified capacity model: 4 GiB, 1 GiB, 0.5 GiB, 0.1875 GiB and 0.2 GiB per sequence. GQA gives 4x over MHA; FP8 doubles it again; 2-bit codes with scales or keeping 20% of tokens give about 5x more.

blocks.md: These levers compose: H2O's paper reports that combining its eviction with quantization did better than either alone in its tests. But each has a different failure mode. Quantization adds small noise everywhere, so check sensitive layers and the first token. Eviction loses tokens permanently, so check retrieval over long contexts. GQA is fixed at training time. FP8 is the low-risk, widely supported option in vLLM and TensorRT-LLM (it must be enabled; vLLM's default `kv_cache_dtype` is `"auto"`, the model's dtype); 2-bit and eviction methods need careful evaluation on your own workload.

Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable.
Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

blocks.question: A RAG service sends 30K-token prompts and generates 200-token answers. Memory is dominated by prompt KV. Which method fits best?
options: SnapKV-style selection after prefill, guided by the end of the prompt
Sliding window over the last 4096 tokens
blocks.explain: The cache is created at once by a long prompt, and the question usually sits at the end. SnapKV uses those final prompt tokens to pick what each head will need. A plain window drops most of the documents.

blocks.question: Why does PyramidKV give lower layers a bigger budget?
options: Higher layers are skipped at inference time
Attention in lower layers is spread over many tokens, while higher layers focus on a few
blocks.explain: Its analysis shows information funneling: broad attention low, concentrated attention high. Uniform budgets waste slots in high layers and starve low ones.

blocks.question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
blocks.explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.
